Record Q3 - revenue up 98% on North American volume growth and a ~60,000 increase in door count (37,000 in convenience).
The PepsiCo distribution partnership officially commenced October 1, 2022; most retail accounts already transitioned, and the transition exceeded initial expectations.
Key milestone: Celsius passed Bang to become the #3 US energy drink (4.9 share vs Bang's 4.4).
Early PepsiCo launch metrics: ~11% ACV gain (~23% in convenience) and items carried per store rising from 7.7 to 8.3 in just three weeks.
Gross margin improved to 41.8% (49.6% ex-freight), up 330 bps sequentially, on improved average can prices and freight; club channel mix continues to pressure margin.
Large transition-related noise items: $155.4M Q3 distributor termination expense (in S&M, funded by Pepsi as deferred revenue amortized over 20 years) plus ~$50M more in Q4.

The $550M preferred was valued at $832.5M; the $282.5M premium recorded as an other asset amortized as contra revenue over 20 years; non-deductibility drove a negative 33.5% nine-month effective tax rate and a $71.4M deferred tax liability.
The FAST bar brand US launch was abandoned (FAST will now be focused internationally), triggering a $2.4M impairment; also a $7.8M class-action settlement.
Management could only offer a 'gut feel' of $15-20M of revenue potentially shifted between Q3 and Q4 due to Pepsi pipe-fill versus distributor inventory wind-down.
Management was non-committal on velocity / sales per point of distribution as Celsius enters lower-awareness new markets and Tier 3/Tier 4 accounts.

Mid-40s Q4 gross margin target framed as a wide 43.5%-47.5% range, with variables including gas prices, softening aluminum, remaining international cans (smaller amount on the West Coast) and product returns.
Spring 2023 retailer resets cited as a major shelf-space opportunity, amplified by Bang's distribution-network disruption.
A number of new flavors will launch in Q1 2023; items per store (~8.6) lags category leaders at 20-30, leaving significant SKU runway.
No additional price increases were taken in Q3; revenue growth was volume-driven; margin benefit came from the orbit model / onboard freight and lower can prices, not pricing.
Celsius expects to be 'in great shape' / 'locked in' on the transition by early Q1 2023; per the Pepsi call it was already 80%+ transitioned on its DSD business.
Go-forward effective tax rate guided to 21% federal plus ~5-6% state; ~50,000 incremental Pepsi energy coolers rolling out now; 13 active co-packers with capacity for years.
How will shelf space evolve as Celsius transitions onto Bang's shelves - one-to-one trade or more space/SKUs - and what about velocity / sales per point of distribution?

SKU/shelf-space gains in just three weeks (largest in convenience); Bang disruption and resets create opportunity for spring resets; non-committal on velocity - entering lower-awareness markets and less-productive Tier 3/Tier 4 accounts, 'can't really give you an answer at this point.'
Noah Erni (on for Kevin Grundy), Jefferies
How much US business has transitioned to PepsiCo, and what is the international expansion timeline?

Already 80%+ transitioned on DSD business per the Pepsi call; a handful more geographies roll out through Q4 into Q1; expects to be 'in great shape' by early Q1; international real but approached methodically with more detail through 2023 (Pepsi distributes across 126 markets).
Pepsi sales impact, Q4 revenue & gross margin
Quantify the one-time versus recurring nature of sales to Pepsi (12.4% of sales per the 10-Q) and Q4 North America growth; are higher-cost cans behind, and is mid-40s an exit rate or Q4 average?

Q3/Q4 will be noisy; 'gut feel' of ~$15-20M potentially shifted between quarters (not data-supported); big Q4/Q1 opportunity from new space and SKU expansion; most international cans cycled through with a smaller amount on the West Coast; Q4 gross margin guided to a 43.5%-47.5% range.
What are the next steps and milestones as the Pepsi DSD ramp moves from Q4 into Q1, and what is left in the club channel / how many Pepsi coolers?

Milestones: convenience expansion (ACV, SKUs/items per store), maintaining velocity, the PepsiCo medals loyalty program, and foodservice; Sam's Club ramping (BJ's room to expand, no cannibalization); ~50,000 Pepsi-owned energy coolers the immediate cooler opportunity.
Confirm the termination expense was paid by Pepsi and shows as deferred revenue, any follow-on costs after Q4, the right SKU count, and whether 13 co-packers is right?

An initial $174.7M tranche was provided by Pepsi, of which $155.4M was accrued (unspent returned), with additional Q4 settlements; expects to be 'locked in' entering 2023; SKU counts vary by retailer (~8.6 nationwide average vs 20-30 for leaders); 13 active co-packers with backups, capacity for years.
Is Pepsi spending direct marketing dollars, and why is Celsius still rolling out its own branded coolers rather than focusing solely on Pepsi's 50,000?

Early in the relationship - opportunities to partner on programs (college sponsorships, co-op promotions, medals program), but pushing the brand/velocity remains Celsius's focus; Celsius-branded coolers are wholly owned 'silent salespersons' with strong ROI, pursued alongside the co-branded/Pepsi energy coolers.
Repeat the tax-noise commentary, what go-forward effective tax rate to use, and were any price increases taken in Q3?

Preferred valued at $832.5M (a $282.5M premium recorded as an asset, amortized as contra revenue over ~20 years, non-deductible) created the timing difference; go-forward effective tax rate ~21% federal plus ~5-6% state; no price increases in Q3 - margin benefit came from the orbit model / onboard freight and lower can prices, not pricing.
